Noninvasive treatment modalities are used for mild or early cases of triggering and in patients who are opposed to injections. Activity modification, especially symptom-provoking activities, should be avoided. Although there is no scientific evidence to support the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), this drug class is commonly recommended to alleviate the local inflammatory response secondary to triggering. Prolonged use, however, may contribute to peptic ulcer disease and kidney failure.
Splinting is a commonly used conservative treatment option with the theoretic concept that limiting tendon gliding allows time for inflammation to resolve (Fig. 2). In a series of 28 patients placed in a metacarpophalangeal (MCP) blocking splint at $10^{\circ}$ to $15^{\circ}$ of flexion for a 6- to 10-week period, Colbourn and colleagues $^{10}$ found that 93% of patients reported improvement in symptoms. Rogers and colleagues $^{11}$ achieved 83% success with a distal interphalangeal joint blocking splint, limiting FDP excursion, in a small series of laborers. Tarbhai and colleagues $^{12}$ compared these 2 splinting techniques in a randomized trial and found a higher percentage of patients had complete or partial relief of symptoms with the MCP blocking splint (77% vs 43%), although it was subjectively reported as more cumbersome. Immobilization is most effective in mild cases of triggering, with
short duration of symptoms, and requires high level of splint compliance. $^{9,13}$
Local corticosteroids are routinely used as a first-line treatment of trigger finger of all severities. Although local steroid injections are more effective compared with a placebo injection, there is a significant number of patients who fail this modality or develop recurrence. $^{14}$ Castellanos and colleagues $^{15}$ performed a review of trigger fingers treated with corticosteroid injections with a mean follow-up of 8 years and found a success rate, defined as resolution of symptoms for at least 36 months, of $69\%$ . A more recent review of the literature found that only $57\%$ of patients had relief with corticosteroid injections. $^{16}$ Rozental and colleagues $^{17}$ found a recurrence of $56\%$ up to 1 year after injections and found that younger age, type 1 diabetes mellitus, involvement of multiple digits, and history of other tendonopathies were associated with a higher rate of treatment failure. Patients with more than 6 months of symptoms are also less likely to have triggering resolution. $^{18}$ The type of steroid has not been shown to affect long-term outcomes. Triamcinolone, however, a non-water-soluble medication, has shown more effective in the short term (6 weeks after administration) when prospectively compared with dexamethasone, a water-soluble steroid. $^{19}$ Appropriate counseling should be provided to patients because patience may be required to see a beneficial effect from the steroid.

When addressing trigger finger, our first line of defense often involves noninvasive strategies. These approaches are particularly well-suited for mild cases, early-stage symptoms, or for patients who prefer to avoid injections. Think of this as a "gentle reset" for the tendon, aiming to calm the irritation without surgical intervention.

The journey begins with **activity modification**. This is a crucial, yet often overlooked, step. The logic is straightforward: if certain movements are provoking your symptoms, we must temporarily avoid them to break the cycle of irritation. Imagine a frayed rope; if you keep pulling it back and forth through a tight hole, the fraying worsens. By stopping the specific activities that cause the "catching" or locking sensation, we give the inflamed tissue a chance to settle down.

You may also hear recommendations for **nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)**, such as ibuprofen or naproxen. Here, it is important to distinguish between common practice and scientific proof. While these medications are frequently suggested to reduce the local inflammatory response caused by the triggering mechanism, we must be transparent: there is currently no rigorous scientific evidence confirming their effectiveness specifically for trigger finger. Nevertheless, they remain a common tool in the clinical toolkit. However, caution is warranted. Just as you wouldn't leave a car engine running indefinitely, you cannot take NSAIDs forever. Prolonged use carries significant risks, including the potential development of peptic ulcer disease (sores in the stomach lining) and even kidney failure. Therefore, if used, they should be part of a short-term strategy rather than a permanent solution.

Another cornerstone of conservative care is **splinting**. The theoretical concept here is elegant in its simplicity: by limiting the gliding motion of the tendon, we essentially put the injured area on "bed rest," allowing the inflammation to resolve naturally (Fig. 2).

Let's look at the evidence to see how this plays out in practice. In a notable study involving 28 patients, Colbourn and colleagues $^{10}$ utilized a specific type of brace called a **metacarpophalangeal (MCP) blocking splint**. To visualize this, imagine a brace that stops your finger from bending at the large knuckle where the finger meets the hand (the MCP joint), holding it slightly bent at $10^{\circ}$ to $15^{\circ}$ of flexion. This position keeps the tendon relatively still without locking the entire finger straight. Patients wore this splint for a period of 6 to 10 weeks. The results were impressive: 93% of patients reported an improvement in their symptoms.

Similarly, Rogers and colleagues $^{11}$ tested a different approach on a small group of laborers. They used a **distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint blocking splint**. This device works differently; instead of stopping motion at the big knuckle, it limits the excursion (movement range) of the **Flexor Digitorum Profundus (FDP)** tendon by blocking the joint nearest the fingertip. This method achieved an 83% success rate.

But which method is superior? Tarbhai and colleagues $^{12}$ designed a randomized trial to compare these two techniques directly. Their findings offer a nuanced lesson in trade-offs. They discovered that the MCP blocking splint (the one holding the big knuckle) provided complete or partial relief to a higher percentage of patients compared to the DIP splint (77% vs. 43%). However, there was a catch: patients subjectively reported the MCP splint as more cumbersome and awkward to wear. This highlights a common challenge in medicine: the most effective treatment isn't always the most comfortable.

Ultimately, immobilization via splinting shines brightest in specific scenarios: mild cases of triggering, situations where symptoms have been present for only a short duration, and critically, when the patient maintains a high level of **splint compliance**. If the splint is frequently removed, the tendon continues to glide and irritate, rendering the treatment ineffective $^{9,13}$.

Moving beyond mechanical restrictions, **local corticosteroids** represent the routine first-line treatment for trigger finger across all levels of severity. You can think of corticosteroids as a powerful "fire extinguisher" for inflammation, delivered directly to the site of the problem. While local steroid injections are demonstrably more effective than a placebo (a fake injection with no active drug), it is vital to manage expectations. A significant number of patients either do not respond to this modality initially or experience a recurrence of symptoms later on $^{14}$.

Let's examine the long-term data to understand the realistic odds. Castellanos and colleagues $^{15}$ conducted a comprehensive review of trigger fingers treated with corticosteroid injections, tracking patients for an average of 8 years. They defined "success" strictly as the resolution of symptoms lasting at least 36 months. Under these rigorous criteria, the success rate was $69\%$. However, a more recent review of the literature suggests the numbers may be shifting, finding that only $57\%$ of patients achieved relief with corticosteroid injections $^{16}$.

Why do some treatments fail? Rozental and colleagues $^{17}$ investigated this by looking at recurrence rates up to one year after injection, finding a recurrence rate of $56\%$. Their analysis revealed specific risk factors that act as red flags for treatment failure. Patients are more likely to experience recurrence if they are of younger age, have type 1 diabetes mellitus, involve multiple digits (fingers), or have a history of other tendonopathies (tendon disorders). Additionally, timing matters: patients who have suffered from symptoms for more than 6 months are less likely to see a permanent resolution of triggering $^{18}$. Essentially, the longer the inflammation persists, the harder it becomes to reverse with injections alone.

Does the specific type of steroid matter? Research indicates that the choice of steroid does not significantly affect long-term outcomes. However, there is a distinction in the short term. Triamcinolone, which is a **non-water-soluble** medication, has shown greater effectiveness in the immediate aftermath (specifically 6 weeks after administration) when compared to dexamethasone, a **water-soluble** steroid $^{19}$. To use an analogy, think of non-water-soluble steroids as a slow-release capsule that stays at the injection site longer, providing a sustained anti-inflammatory effect, whereas water-soluble versions may dissipate more quickly.

Finally, appropriate counseling is paramount. Patients must be informed that patience is a virtue in this treatment path. The beneficial effects of the steroid are not always instantaneous; it may take time for the inflammation to subside and for the smooth gliding of the tendon to be restored.

> **Teacher's Note:** Let's pause to visualize this. Imagine the finger tendons are like ropes running through a series of rings (pulleys) to keep them close to the bone. In rheumatoid arthritis, the lining around these ropes becomes inflamed (tenosynovitis). The "FDS slip" is a specific part of the flexor digitorum superficialis tendon. By removing (resecting) this specific slip, surgeons reduce the bulk and friction inside the tunnel, preventing the inflammation from coming back. It's an extra safety step specifically for these patients, done alongside the main procedure of cutting the first ring (the A1 pulley).

Percutaneous release of the A1 pulley was first described in 1958 and has increased in popularity over the past 2 decades. $^{36}$ The procedure involves releasing the A1 pulley under local anesthesia with the use of a large bore needle or tenotome while the patient intentionally triggers the affected finger. Immediate symptom resolution should be directly observed with a successful procedure. Understanding anatomic landmarks is pivotal in avoiding injury to the neurovascular bundles (Fig. 4). Several guides based on cutaneous
landmarks have been supported to determine the safest trajectory for insertion of a cutting guide. $^{37-39}$ Although the percutaneous technique has been shown effective and safe for the thumb, many advocates avoid performing the procedure on the thumb because the digital nerve courses over the A1 pulley. $^{40}$

> **Deep Dive: The "Why" and "How" of Percutaneous Release**
>
> *   **What does "Percutaneous" mean?** Literally "through the skin." Instead of making a large incision to open up the hand, the surgeon uses a needle or a small blade to cut the tight pulley from the outside. Think of it like popping a balloon through a tiny pinprick rather than cutting it open with scissors.
> *   **The Strategy of Active Triggering:** Why does the text say the patient must "intentionally trigger" the finger during the cut? This is a brilliant feedback loop. As the surgeon cuts the tight A1 pulley, the patient moves the finger. If the catching or locking (triggering) stops *immediately*, the surgeon knows the job is done. It's a real-time quality control check.
> *   **The Danger Zone (Neurovascular Bundles):** This is critical. Running right next to those tendons are the nerves (which feel sensation) and arteries (which supply blood). These are the "neurovascular bundles." If the needle slips, it could sever a nerve, causing permanent numbness. This is why knowing the exact "anatomic landmarks"—the invisible map of where these structures lie under the skin—is non-negotiable.
> *   **The Thumb Dilemma:** You might wonder, "If it works for fingers, why not the thumb?" The anatomy of the thumb is trickier. In many people, the digital nerve doesn't just run *next* to the A1 pulley; it actually crosses *over* it. Trying to cut the pulley with a blind needle strike is like trying to cut a rope that has a live wire draped across it—the risk of hitting the nerve is simply too high for many surgeons, despite the technique being theoretically possible.

Ragoowansi and colleagues $^{41}$ performed percutaneous A1 release on 180 patients and 95% had symptom resolution. Ha and colleagues $^{42}$ had similar success in 185 patients, 94% success, after percutaneous release with a specially designed hooked knife. A recent meta-analysis of more than 2100 percutaneous A1 pulley releases found a success rate of 94% with only 4 major complications: 2 infections, 1 fixed flexion deformity, and 1 permanent digital nerve injury. $^{43}$ In this review, there was no difference in results found when comparing a large bore needle to a cutting instrument or if cortisone was concomitantly used. The use of sonography during the procedure led to significantly higher success compared with the procedures done without the adjunct use of this imaging modality, 99% and 94%, respectively (P = .010).

> **Interpreting the Data: What Do These Numbers Tell Us?**
>
> *   **Consistency is Key:** Notice how different studies (Ragoowansi, Ha, and the massive meta-analysis) all converge on a success rate around 94–95%. When multiple independent groups find the same result, it gives us high confidence that the procedure is reliably effective.
> *   **Safety Profile:** Out of more than 2,100 procedures, there were only 4 *major* complications. That is an incredibly low risk profile. However, note the nature of those complications: infection, stiffness (fixed flexion), and nerve injury. These remind us that even "minimally invasive" procedures carry real risks if not performed with care.
> *   **Tool Choice Doesn't Matter (Much):** The analysis found no difference between using a thick needle versus a specialized hooked knife. This suggests the *technique* and the *surgeon's skill* are more important than the specific tool. Similarly, adding cortisone (a steroid to reduce inflammation) at the same time didn't change the outcome.
> *   **The Power of Seeing (Sonography):** Here is a game-changer. "Sonography" means using ultrasound imaging. When surgeons used ultrasound to *see* the needle and the pulley in real-time, success jumped from 94% to 99%. The P-value (.010) tells us this isn't a lucky fluke; it's a statistically significant improvement. It's the difference between cutting in the dark versus cutting with a flashlight.

Calleja and colleagues $^{44}$ performed 25 trigger finger releases using percutaneous technique, immediately followed by open exploration, to determine how much of the A1 pulley had been released. All patients in this series had complete relief of triggering symptoms after the percutaneous procedure before the open procedure was performed. Only 24% of these digits had complete release of the A1 pulley after the minimally invasive approach; 15 of 25 had incomplete, superficial tendon injuries that were not clinically significant.

> **A Fascinating Paradox: Less is More?**
>
> This study design is clever. The surgeons did the needle release, confirmed the finger worked perfectly, and *then* immediately opened the hand up to see what actually happened inside.
>
> *   **The Surprise:** Even though 100% of the patients felt cured, the surgeons found that the A1 pulley was *fully* cut in only 24% of cases. In other words, in 76% of patients, the pulley was only partially cut, yet the triggering stopped!
> *   **The Lesson:** This teaches us that we don't necessarily need to destroy the entire pulley to fix the problem. Perhaps weakening it just enough allows the tendon to glide smoothly again.
> *   **The Trade-off:** There were minor scratches (superficial injuries) on the tendons in 15 out of 25 cases. The text notes these were "not clinically significant," meaning they didn't cause pain or weakness. However, it serves as a reminder that the needle is blindly scraping against the tendon; it's a trade-off between a tiny, harmless scratch and the benefit of avoiding a large surgical scar.

PEDIATRIC TRIGGER DIGIT
The pathology, natural progression, and management of pediatric trigger fingers and trigger thumbs differ significantly from their adult counterparts. Commonly, children are brought in by their parents, at approximately 2 years of age, with the observation that a child has a flexed posture of the thumb or an inability to extend the thumb at the interphalangeal joint. Careful examination of the contralateral hand should be performed because 25% of children have bilateral involvement. $^{45}$ A nodule is usually present and palpable on the FPL tendon. This is termed, Notta nodule, after the physician who first described it. $^{46}$

> **Shifting Gears: Children Are Not Small Adults**
>
> It is a common mistake in medicine to assume a child's condition is just a smaller version of an adult's. Here, the rules change completely.
>
> *   **The Presentation:** While adults often complain of painful clicking, parents of toddlers (around age 2) usually notice something visual: the thumb is stuck bent (flexed) and won't straighten out at the tip joint (the interphalangeal joint).
> *   **Check Both Hands:** Because 25% (1 in 4) of these children have it in *both* hands, a smart clinician never looks at just the problematic hand. Always check the "contralateral" (opposite) hand, even if the parent didn't mention it.
> *   **The Notta Nodule:** If you feel the tendon on the palm side of the thumb, you will often feel a distinct bump. This is the "Notta nodule." Think of it like a knot in a rope that has gotten too big to pass smoothly through the pulley ring. It's named after the doctor who first identified this specific swelling in children.

The etiology behind pediatric trigger fingers and thumbs remains largely unknown. Microscopic analysis of biopsied A1 pulleys and Notta nodules from pediatric thumbs have depicted large amounts of mature collagen and fibroblasts

without evidence of infectious, inflammatory, or degenerative changes. $^{47}$

Instead, the root cause lies in a specific biological process: a **fibrous proliferation**. Let's pause to unpack this term. "Fibrous" refers to the formation of tough, scar-like tissue, and "proliferation" means rapid growth or multiplication. Imagine a hallway (the tendon sheath) that suddenly has thick, fuzzy carpeting installed on the walls; the person trying to walk through (the tendon) now gets stuck.

evidence has failed to support the belief that pediatric trigger finger is a congenital condition. $^{48,49}$ The term, congenital trigger finger, is now considered a misnomer and the trigger finger in this patient population is considered an acquired pathology. $^{50}$

The etiology of pediatric trigger finger, a much less common condition than trigger thumb, seems more complex and multifactorial. Nodularity of the FDS and FDP, constriction of the A1-A3 pulleys, and proximal decussation of the FDS are causes of triggering. $^{51}$ Trigger finger, in this age group, has been associated with congenital metabolic and inflammatory disorders, but a majority of cases are idiopathic. There is no consensus regarding the natural history of this condition available in the literature.
Surgical intervention of pediatric trigger thumb is not always necessary because the natural

Recent scientific evidence has fundamentally shifted our understanding of this condition in children. For

long time, doctors believed pediatric trigger finger was a **congenital** condition, meaning the child was born with it due to an error in development within the womb. However, new data has failed to support this belief. $^{48,49}$ Consequently, the term "congenital trigger finger" is now considered a **misnomer**—a name that is incorrect or misleading. The current medical consensus is that trigger finger in this young patient population is actually an **acquired pathology**, meaning it develops after birth due to factors that occur during the child's growth. $^{50}$

The **etiology** (the study of causes or origins) of pediatric *trigger finger* (affecting the fingers, not just the thumb) is a much less common condition than trigger *thumb*, and its origins appear far more complex and **multifactorial**. "Multifactorial" is a crucial concept here; it tells us there isn't just one single culprit. Instead, several distinct structural issues can combine to cause the problem:
*   **Nodularity of the FDS and FDP:** The Flexor Digitorum Superficialis (FDS) and Flexor Digitorum Profundus (FDP) tendons may develop lumps or knots (nodules), much like a rope that has frayed and bunched up.
*   **Constriction of the A1-A3 pulleys:** Instead of just the first ring (A1) being tight, multiple rings (A1 through A3) may be narrowed.
*   **Proximal decussation of the FDS:** This is a fancy way of describing how the FDS tendon splits and crosses over itself near its origin. If this crossing point is abnormal, it can create friction.
These structural anomalies are primary causes of triggering. $^{51}$ Furthermore, trigger finger in this age group has been associated with underlying congenital metabolic and inflammatory disorders (systemic conditions affecting how the body processes energy or fights inflammation). However, it is important to note that the majority of cases are **idiopathic**. In medicine, "idiopathic" is a humble admission: it means "we don't know the specific cause." Despite looking for a reason, most cases arise spontaneously without a clear underlying disease. Currently, there is no consensus in the medical literature regarding the **natural history** of this condition—essentially, we lack a definitive map of how the disease progresses over time if left completely untreated.

Surgical intervention for pediatric trigger *thumb* is not always immediately necessary. Why? Because the natural history suggests that a majority of cases will resolve on their own, albeit over a long period of time. Think of it as a slow-growing child eventually outgrowing a tight shoe. A review of 26 pediatric trigger thumbs provided some concrete numbers: only 12% resolved by 6 months, but that number jumped significantly to 73% by 12 months after the child first presented to the doctor. $^{45}$ A more recent, larger review of 71 pediatric trigger thumbs confirmed this trend, finding that 63% resolved without any surgical intervention. However, patience is key: the median time to resolution was a substantial 48 months (4 years). $^{52}$

Despite knowing that many cases heal spontaneously, it remains unclear whether specific variables—such as the severity of the locking, the age of the child, or other factors—can predict which children will get better on their own and which will not. In the meantime, doctors have tried conservative (non-surgical) treatments. These include **therapy** (guided movement), **passive extension exercises** (gently straightening the finger for the child), and **splinting** (wearing a brace to keep the finger straight). These methods have shown some improvement in symptoms and increased the range of motion at the **interphalangeal joint** (the joint in the middle of the finger). Yet, a major question remains unanswered: are these active treatments truly superior to mere **observation** (simply watching and waiting)? The data is not yet definitive. $^{53,54}$ Given this uncertainty, it is the authors' clinical practice to recommend surgical intervention specifically for the **toddler population**, particularly if a **fixed flexion deformity** is present. A fixed flexion deformity means the finger is permanently stuck in a bent position and cannot be straightened even with help. The reasoning here is practical: toddlers are an unlikely cohort to be compliant with the rigorous demands of wearing a splint or performing therapy exercises, making non-surgical approaches often futile.

Surgery is usually performed under **general anesthesia** in this patient population, ensuring the child is completely asleep and feels no pain.
